title: Αἰγὶς καὶ ἠήρ
titleEn: The Aegis and the Mist — Iliad 17.582–672
about: Apollo, in the likeness of Hector’s guest-friend Phaenops, taunts Hector for shrinking from Menelaus, and Hector goes back into the front rank. Zeus then takes his tasselled aegis, covers Ida in cloud, thunders, and gives the Trojans the upper hand, and the Achaeans break and flee. Hector casts at Idomeneus and misses; his spear kills Coeranus, Meriones’ charioteer, who had driven up to save Idomeneus, and Meriones tells Idomeneus to whip for the ships. Ajax sees Zeus’ hand in it and urges the others to find a plan to bring the body home, but the Achaeans are lost in mist, and he prays that Zeus clear the air, if he must destroy them, then at least in daylight. Zeus pities him and the battle comes into view. Ajax sends Menelaus to find Antilochus and have him carry the news to Achilles. Menelaus leaves the body like a lion driven from the farmyard, and charges Meriones and the two Ajaxes to remember Patroclus’ kindness.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτορα δ’ ἐγγύθεν ἱστάμενος ὄτρυνεν Ἀπόλλων
Φαίνοπι Ἀσιάδῃ ἐναλίγκιος, ὅς οἱ ἁπάντων
ξείνων φίλτατος ἔσκεν Ἀβυδόθι οἰκία ναίων·
sentences.i: Apollo stood close beside Hector and urged him on, like Phaenops, son of Asius, who of all his guest-friends was dearest to him and lived in a house at Abydus;
sentences.n: Apollo is the subject, and his name comes last: ἐγγύθεν ἱστάμενος is ‘taking his stand close by’, and ὄτρυνεν is the aorist of ὀτρύνω ‘urge on’. Ἀσιάδῃ is a patronymic, ‘son of Asius’, in the dative after ἐναλίγκιος ‘like’. In ὅς οἱ ἁπάντων … φίλτατος ἔσκεν ‘who was dearest to him of all’, οἱ is Hector, and ἔσκεν is an old form of ἦν ‘was’. ξείνων is ‘guest-friends’, men bound by hospitality. Ἀβυδόθι is ‘at Abydus’, a town on the Hellespont, with the ending -θι for ‘at’; οἰκία ναίων is ‘living in a house’, with οἰκία (a neuter plural, ‘dwellings’) as the object of ναίων ‘inhabiting’.

sentences.t: τῷ μιν ἐεισάμενος προσέφη ἑκάεργος Ἀπόλλων·
sentences.l: Having made himself like to that man, addressed him far-working Apollo:
sentences.i: Making himself like that man, Apollo, who works from afar, said to him:
sentences.n: τῷ is the article used as a pronoun, ‘that man’ (Phaenops), in the dative after ἐεισάμενος, the aorist participle of the verb for ‘make oneself like’; μιν is Hector. προσέφη is the aorist of πρόσφημι ‘speak to’. ἑκάεργος ‘far-working’ is a stock epithet of Apollo, translated the same way every time; its exact sense is disputed.

sentences.t: Ἕκτορ τίς κέ σ’ ἔτ’ ἄλλος Ἀχαιῶν ταρβήσειεν;
sentences.l: “Hector, who else of the Achaeans would any longer be terrified of you?
sentences.i: “Hector, who else among the Achaeans would be terrified of you any longer?
sentences.n: A scornful question from the god in disguise. ταρβήσειεν is the aorist optative of ταρβέω ‘be terrified of’, which with κε gives ‘would be terrified’, and σ’ is σε ‘you’. The point comes in the next line: Hector has just shrunk from Menelaus.

sentences.t:
οἷον δὴ Μενέλαον ὑπέτρεσας, ὃς τὸ πάρος γε
μαλθακὸς αἰχμητής·
sentences.l:
Such a Menelaus you took fright at, who in the past, at least,
was a soft spearman;
sentences.i: You took fright at such a man as Menelaus, who in the past, at least, was a soft spearman;
sentences.n: οἷον … Μενέλαον ‘such a Menelaus’ is said with scorn, and is the object of ὑπέτρεσας, the aorist of ὑποτρέω ‘take fright at, shrink in fear before’. ὃς τὸ πάρος γε ‘who in the past, at least’ has no verb of its own, and ‘was’ is understood. μαλθακός ‘soft’ means unwarlike, and αἰχμητής is ‘spearman’, so the claim is that Menelaus used to be no fighter.

sentences.t:
νῦν δ’ οἴχεται οἶος ἀείρας
νεκρὸν ὑπ’ ἐκ Τρώων, σὸν δ’ ἔκτανε πιστὸν ἑταῖρον
ἐσθλὸν ἐνὶ προμάχοισι Ποδῆν υἱὸν Ἠετίωνος.
sentences.l:
but now he is gone, alone, having lifted
the corpse from under the Trojans, and he has killed your trusty companion,
a good one among the front-fighters, Podes, son of Eetion.”
sentences.i: but now he has gone off alone, having lifted the corpse away from under the Trojans, and he has killed your trusty companion, a good man among the foremost fighters, Podes, son of Eetion.”
sentences.n: οἴχεται, from οἴχομαι, is ‘is gone’, and οἶος is ‘alone’. ἀείρας is the aorist participle of ἀείρω ‘lift’, and νεκρὸν ὑπ’ ἐκ Τρώων ‘the corpse from under the Trojans’ looks back to the end of the previous part, where Menelaus kills Podes and drags the body off. Podes is the accusative object of ἔκτανε ‘killed’ (aorist of κτείνω), with σὸν … πιστὸν ἑταῖρον ‘your trusty companion’ and ἐσθλόν ‘good’ beside him. Ἠετίωνος is the genitive of Ἠετίων, the name of Andromache’s father too; nothing here says they are the same man.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, τὸν δ’ ἄχεος νεφέλη ἐκάλυψε μέλαινα,
βῆ δὲ διὰ προμάχων κεκορυθμένος αἴθοπι χαλκῷ.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and him a cloud of grief covered, dark,
and he went through the front-fighters, armed with the fire-faced bronze.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and a dark cloud of grief covered Hector; and he went through the foremost fighters, armed with bronze that has the look of fire.
sentences.n: The first line is a formula for a man struck by sudden grief: ‘a cloud of grief covered him, dark’, ἄχεος being the genitive of ἄχος ‘grief’; the Odyssey has the same line. The second line is the stock line of a warrior going to the front: κεκορυθμένος, from κορύσσω ‘arm’, is a perfect participle, ‘armed’; προμάχων is ‘front-fighters’; αἴθοπι, from αἴθοψ, means ‘fire-faced’, ‘with the look of fire’.

sentences.t:
καὶ τότ’ ἄρα Κρονίδης ἕλετ’ αἰγίδα θυσσανόεσσαν
μαρμαρέην, Ἴδην δὲ κατὰ νεφέεσσι κάλυψεν,
ἀστράψας δὲ μάλα μεγάλ’ ἔκτυπε, τὴν δὲ τίναξε,
νίκην δὲ Τρώεσσι δίδου, ἐφόβησε δ’ Ἀχαιούς.
sentences.l:
And then the son-of-Cronus took the tasselled aegis,
gleaming, and Ida with clouds he covered over,
and having lightened, very greatly he thundered, and shook it,
and victory he was giving to the Trojans, and put the Achaeans to flight.
sentences.i: Then the son of Cronus took the tasselled aegis, gleaming, and covered Ida with clouds; he flashed lightning, thundered mightily, and shook the aegis, and he was giving victory to the Trojans and put the Achaeans to flight.
sentences.n: Κρονίδης ‘son of Cronus’ is Zeus. The aegis is his tasselled cloak or shield of storm, and θυσσανόεσσαν ‘tasselled’ and μαρμαρέην ‘gleaming’ both agree with it. Ἴδην … κατὰ … κάλυψεν is tmesis, a preposition split from its verb: κατακαλύπτω ‘cover over’, with νεφέεσσι ‘with clouds’; Ida is the mountain near Troy. ἀστράψας is the aorist participle of ἀστράπτω ‘flash lightning’, and ἔκτυπε the aorist of κτυπέω ‘crash’, here of thunder. τὴν is the aegis again. δίδου is an imperfect without the augment, ‘was giving’.

sentences.t: πρῶτος Πηνέλεως Βοιώτιος ἦρχε φόβοιο.
sentences.l: First Peneleos the Boeotian began the flight.
sentences.i: Peneleos the Boeotian was the first to begin the flight.
sentences.n: A new paragraph: the sign of Zeus takes effect. ἦρχε φόβοιο ‘began the flight’ has ἄρχω with the genitive, and φόβος in battle is ‘flight’, not ‘fear’. Βοιώτιος is ‘Boeotian’, an adjective telling you which Peneleos.

sentences.t:
βλῆτο γὰρ ὦμον δουρὶ πρόσω τετραμμένος αἰεὶ
ἄκρον ἐπιλίγδην·
sentences.l:
For he was hit on the shoulder by a spear, always turned forward,
at the top, grazingly;
sentences.i: for he was hit on the shoulder by a spear, always facing forward, at the top, with a grazing blow;
sentences.n: βλῆτο is a root aorist of βάλλω with passive sense and no augment, ‘was hit’. ὦμον ‘on the shoulder’ is the accusative of the part struck. πρόσω τετραμμένος αἰεί ‘always turned forward’ means facing the enemy, so this is a wound from the front. ἄκρον ‘at the top’ goes with the shoulder; ἐπιλίγδην is a rare word, and ‘grazingly’ is the sense taken from γράψεν in the next line.

sentences.t:
γράψεν δέ οἱ ὀστέον ἄχρις
αἰχμὴ Πουλυδάμαντος·
sentences.l:
and scratched for him, right to the bone,
the point of Polydamas;
sentences.i: and the point of Polydamas’ spear scratched him right to the bone;
sentences.n: γράψεν is the aorist of γράφω ‘scratch, scrape’, the verb that later also means ‘write’; οἱ is ‘him’. αἰχμή is the ‘point’ of the spear and is the subject. In ὀστέον ἄχρις, ‘right to the bone’ is the sense taken, but the grammar is not quite clear: ὀστέον could instead be the object of γράψεν, with ἄχρις an adverb ‘utterly’.

sentences.t: ὃ γάρ ῥ’ ἔβαλε σχεδὸν ἐλθών.
sentences.l: for he it was who hit him, having come near.
sentences.i: for it was he who had hit him, after coming up close.
sentences.n: ὃ is the article used as a pronoun, ‘he’, that is Polydamas, and γάρ explains why the point is called his. ῥ’ is ῥα, a particle that marks the explanation as obvious; ἔβαλε is the aorist of βάλλω ‘hit’, and σχεδὸν ἐλθών ‘having come near’ says the blow came from close range.

sentences.t:
Λήϊτον αὖθ’ Ἕκτωρ σχεδὸν οὔτασε χεῖρ’ ἐπὶ καρπῷ
υἱὸν Ἀλεκτρυόνος μεγαθύμου, παῦσε δὲ χάρμης·
sentences.l:
Leitus in turn Hector wounded from near, on the hand at the wrist,
the son of great-hearted Alectryon, and made him cease from the joy of battle;
sentences.i: Hector in turn wounded Leitus, the son of great-hearted Alectryon, from close by, on the hand at the wrist, and made him cease from the joy of battle;
sentences.n: Hector is the subject, though his name falls in the middle of the line; Λήϊτον is the object and υἱὸν Ἀλεκτρυόνος ‘son of Alectryon’ stands beside it. οὔτασε is the aorist of οὐτάω ‘wound’. χεῖρ’ ἐπὶ καρπῷ ‘on the hand at the wrist’ is the accusative of the part wounded plus a dative of place. παῦσε … χάρμης ‘made him cease from the joy of battle’: παύω takes the genitive, and χάρμη, ‘joy of battle’, is translated the same way every time.

sentences.t:
τρέσσε δὲ παπτήνας, ἐπεὶ οὐκέτι ἔλπετο θυμῷ
ἔγχος ἔχων ἐν χειρὶ μαχήσεσθαι Τρώεσσιν.
sentences.l:
and he took fright, glancing about, since no longer did he hope in his heart,
holding a spear in his hand, to fight with the Trojans.
sentences.i: and he took fright, glancing about, since he no longer hoped in his heart to go on fighting the Trojans with a spear in his hand.
sentences.n: Leitus is still the subject. τρέσσε is an aorist without the augment, ‘took fright’ (τρέω); παπτήνας is the aorist participle of παπταίνω ‘glance about’. ἔλπετο is the imperfect of ἔλπομαι ‘hope’, followed by the future infinitive μαχήσεσθαι ‘to fight’ and the dative Τρώεσσιν; ἔγχος ἔχων ἐν χειρί is ‘holding a spear in his hand’.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτορα δ’ Ἰδομενεὺς μετὰ Λήϊτον ὁρμηθέντα
βεβλήκει θώρηκα κατὰ στῆθος παρὰ μαζόν·
sentences.l:
And Hector, rushing after Leitus, Idomeneus
had hit on the breastplate, at the chest beside the breast;
sentences.i: Idomeneus had hit Hector, as he rushed after Leitus, on the breastplate, at the chest beside the breast;
sentences.n: Idomeneus is the subject, and the word order puts Hector first. ὁρμηθέντα is the aorist passive participle of ὁρμάω ‘rush’, and μετὰ Λήϊτον is ‘after Leitus’. βεβλήκει is the pluperfect of βάλλω ‘had hit’. θώρηκα ‘breastplate’ and μαζόν ‘breast’ are accusatives, with κατὰ στῆθος παρὰ μαζόν ‘at the chest beside the breast’. The next line shows that the blow did not go through.

sentences.t:
ἐν καυλῷ δ’ ἐάγη δολιχὸν δόρυ, τοὶ δὲ βόησαν
Τρῶες·
sentences.l:
At the stem broke the long spear, and shouted
the Trojans;
sentences.i: The long spear broke at the stem, and the Trojans gave a shout;
sentences.n: ἐν καυλῷ ‘at the stem’: καυλός is ‘stem, stalk’, and of a spear the shaft where it meets the blade is probably meant, but the exact place is not certain. ἐάγη is the aorist passive of ἄγνυμι ‘break’; the spear is Idomeneus’, broken on Hector’s breastplate. τοί is the article used as a pronoun, ‘they’, with Τρῶες added after it, and βόησαν is the aorist of βοάω ‘shout’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of the line.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ Ἰδομενῆος ἀκόντισε Δευκαλίδαο
δίφρῳ ἐφεσταότος· τοῦ μέν ῥ’ ἀπὸ τυτθὸν ἅμαρτεν·
sentences.l:
and he at Idomeneus cast, Deucalion’s-son,
standing on the chariot; him, indeed, by a little he missed;
sentences.i: and he cast at Idomeneus, the son of Deucalion, who was standing on his chariot, but missed him by a little;
sentences.n: ὃ is Hector. ἀκόντισε ‘cast’ takes the genitive Ἰδομενῆος for the man aimed at, and Δευκαλίδαο, a patronymic like Ἀτρεΐδης, means ‘son of Deucalion’. δίφρῳ ἐφεσταότος ‘standing on the chariot’ is the perfect participle of ἐφίστημι. ἀπὸ … ἅμαρτεν is ἀφαμαρτάνω ‘miss’ split by tmesis, and τυτθόν is ‘by a little’; μέν looks forward to the αὐτάρ of the next line.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὃ Μηριόναο ὀπάονά θ’ ἡνίοχόν τε
Κοίρανον, ὅς ῥ’ ἐκ Λύκτου ἐϋκτιμένης ἕπετ’ αὐτῷ·
sentences.l:
but he at Meriones’ follower and charioteer,
Coeranus, who from well-built Lyctus followed him;
sentences.i: but he cast at Meriones’ follower and charioteer, Coeranus, who had followed him from well-built Lyctus;
sentences.n: There is no verb in the first line: ἀκόντισε ‘cast’ carries on from the line before, so Hector’s cast now goes at Coeranus. ὀπάονα ‘follower’ and ἡνίοχον ‘charioteer’ are two words for one man, and Μηριόναο is the epic genitive of Μηριόνης (Attic -ου). αὐτῷ in ἕπετ’ αὐτῷ ‘followed him’ is Meriones. Lyctus is a town in Crete, where Coeranus came from, and ἐϋκτιμένης ‘well-built’ is a common epithet of towns. Line 610 is metrically irregular as transmitted: the syllable να of Μηριόναο, which stands in the long place of the third foot, has to be counted long.

sentences.t:
πεζὸς γὰρ τὰ πρῶτα λιπὼν νέας ἀμφιελίσσας
ἤλυθε, καί κε Τρωσὶ μέγα κράτος ἐγγυάλιξεν,
εἰ μὴ Κοίρανος ὦκα ποδώκεας ἤλασεν ἵππους·
sentences.i: for he had come on foot at first, leaving the ships, curved on both sides; and Hector would have put great strength into the hands of the Trojans, if Coeranus had not quickly driven up the fleet-footed horses;
sentences.n: The γάρ explains how Coeranus came to be there: πεζός ‘on foot’, τὰ πρῶτα ‘at first’, and ἤλυθε is the epic form of ἦλθε ‘came’. ἀμφιελίσσας ‘curved on both sides’ is the stock epithet of ships. καί κε … ἐγγυάλιξεν ‘would have put into the hands’ has κε with the aorist for what would have happened, and εἰ μή ‘if … had not’ gives the condition. The subject of ἐγγυάλιξεν is not stated; the condition points to Hector, who by killing Idomeneus would have given the Trojans great strength, and the English names him on that reading. ποδώκεας ‘fleet-footed’ is from ποδώκης.

sentences.t:
καὶ τῷ μὲν φάος ἦλθεν, ἄμυνε δὲ νηλεὲς ἦμαρ,
αὐτὸς δ’ ὤλεσε θυμὸν ὑφ’ Ἕκτορος ἀνδροφόνοιο·
sentences.l:
and to him light came, and he warded off the pitiless day,
but he himself lost his life by man-slaying Hector;
sentences.i: and so for Idomeneus the light of safety came, as Coeranus warded the pitiless day off him; but he himself lost his life at the hands of man-slaying Hector;
sentences.n: The subjects change without being named. τῷ is Idomeneus: φάος, ‘light’, stands for rescue and life. ἄμυνε is the imperfect of ἀμύνω ‘ward off’, with Coeranus as its subject and νηλεὲς ἦμαρ ‘the pitiless day’, the day of death, as its object. αὐτὸς δ’ ‘but he himself’ is Coeranus, who ὤλεσε θυμόν ‘lost his life’ (literally ‘destroyed his spirit’) ὑφ’ Ἕκτορος ‘at the hands of Hector’. ἀνδροφόνοιο ‘man-slaying’ is a stock epithet, translated every time.

sentences.t:
τὸν βάλ’ ὑπὸ γναθμοῖο καὶ οὔατος, ἐκ δ’ ἄρ’ ὀδόντας
ὦσε δόρυ πρυμνόν, διὰ δὲ γλῶσσαν τάμε μέσσην.
sentences.l:
Him he hit under the jaw and the ear, and out the teeth
pushed the spear, hindmost, and through the tongue cut, in the middle.
sentences.i: He hit him under the jaw and the ear, and the spear drove the teeth out, going in all the way, and cut through the middle of his tongue.
sentences.n: This is Hector’s cast told in full: τὸν is Coeranus and βάλ’ is ἔβαλε ‘hit’, with ὑπὸ γναθμοῖο καὶ οὔατος ‘under the jaw and the ear’ (genitives). ἐκ … ὦσε is tmesis, ἐξῶσε ‘pushed out’, from ὠθέω. πρυμνόν is ‘hindmost, at the base’, and with δόρυ its sense is not certain: ‘going in all the way’ is the guess taken. The spear is the subject of τάμε, the aorist of τέμνω ‘cut’ without the augment, and μέσσην agrees with γλῶσσαν, so ‘the tongue, in the middle’.

sentences.t: ἤριπε δ’ ἐξ ὀχέων, κατὰ δ’ ἡνία χεῦεν ἔραζε.
sentences.l: He crashed down from the chariot, and the reins he poured down to the ground.
sentences.i: He crashed down from the chariot and spilled the reins to the ground.
sentences.n: ἤριπε is the aorist of ἐρείπω ‘crash down’, and ἐξ ὀχέων is ‘out of the chariot’, with the plural for one vehicle. κατὰ … χεῦεν is tmesis: χεῦεν is ἔχευεν, the aorist of χέω ‘pour’, so the reins are ‘poured down’, and ἔραζε is ‘to the ground’.

sentences.t:
καὶ τά γε Μηριόνης ἔλαβεν χείρεσσι φίλῃσι
κύψας ἐκ πεδίοιο, καὶ Ἰδομενῆα προσηύδα·
sentences.l:
And these Meriones took in his dear hands,
stooping from the plain, and he addressed Idomeneus:
sentences.i: Meriones picked them up in his own hands, stooping from the plain, and addressed Idomeneus:
sentences.n: τά γε ‘these’ are the reins (ἡνία, neuter plural) just spilled. ἔλαβεν is the aorist of λαμβάνω ‘take’. χείρεσσι φίλῃσι ‘with his dear hands’, where φίλος is ‘his own’; κύψας is the aorist participle of κύπτω ‘stoop’, and πεδίοιο is the epic genitive of πεδίον ‘plain’. προσηύδα is the imperfect of προσαυδάω ‘address’.

sentences.t: μάστιε νῦν εἷός κε θοὰς ἐπὶ νῆας ἵκηαι·
sentences.l: “Whip now, until you come to the swift ships;
sentences.i: “Whip the horses now, until you reach the swift ships;
sentences.n: Meriones speaks. μάστιε is the imperative of μαστίζω ‘whip’, with the horses understood. εἷός κε … ἵκηαι ‘until you reach’: εἷος is ἕως ‘until’, and ἵκηαι is an aorist subjunctive of ἱκνέομαι ‘come to’. θοάς ‘swift’ is the stock adjective of ships.

sentences.t: γιγνώσκεις δὲ καὶ αὐτὸς ὅ τ’ οὐκέτι κάρτος Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.l: and you yourself also know that no longer is the strength of the Achaeans.”
sentences.i: and you yourself know that the strength of the Achaeans is no more.”
sentences.n: ὅ τ’ is ὅ τε, the old ‘that’ (Attic ὅτι), introducing what Idomeneus knows. κάρτος is the epic form of κράτος ‘strength’. The clause has no verb: ‘the strength of the Achaeans is no longer’. καὶ αὐτός is ‘you yourself too’.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφατ’, Ἰδομενεὺς δ’ ἵμασεν καλλίτριχας ἵππους
νῆας ἔπι γλαφυράς· δὴ γὰρ δέος ἔμπεσε θυμῷ.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and Idomeneus lashed the fair-maned horses
to the hollow ships; for fear fell upon his heart.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Idomeneus lashed his fair-maned horses on towards the hollow ships; for fear had fallen upon his heart.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’ closes the speech. ἵμασεν is the aorist of ἱμάσσω ‘lash’ (from ἱμάς ‘strap’), and καλλίτριχας ‘fair-maned’ and γλαφυράς ‘hollow’ are stock epithets. ἔπι follows its noun: νῆας ἔπι is ‘to the ships’. δὴ γάρ gives the reason: δέος is ‘fear’, and ἔμπεσε is the aorist of ἐμπίπτω ‘fall into’.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἔλαθ’ Αἴαντα μεγαλήτορα καὶ Μενέλαον
Ζεύς, ὅτε δὴ Τρώεσσι δίδου ἑτεραλκέα νίκην.
sentences.l:
And did not escape Ajax the great-spirited and Menelaus
Zeus, when indeed to the Trojans he was giving a victory, other-strengthening.
sentences.i: Zeus did not escape the notice of great-spirited Ajax and Menelaus when he was giving the Trojans a victory that turns the fight to the other side.
sentences.n: A new paragraph and a new scene. Zeus is the subject, and οὐδ’ ἔλαθ’ … Ζεύς is ‘Zeus did not escape the notice of’: λανθάνω takes the accusative of those who do not notice, here Αἴαντα and Μενέλαον, so they see that he is helping the Trojans. μεγαλήτορα ‘great-spirited’ is an epithet used of several heroes. ἑτεραλκέα νίκην ‘a victory that turns the fight to the other side’ is built on ἕτερος ‘other’ and ἀλκή ‘strength’, and is translated as it has been in earlier parts. δίδου is an imperfect without the augment.

sentences.t: τοῖσι δὲ μύθων ἦρχε μέγας Τελαμώνιος Αἴας·
sentences.l: And among them of speeches made-beginning great Telamonian Ajax:
sentences.i: Great Telamonian Ajax was the first to speak among them:
sentences.n: A speech-introduction formula: τοῖσι ‘among them’ and μύθων ἦρχε, literally ‘began of speeches’, with ἄρχω taking the genitive, ‘was the first to speak’. Τελαμώνιος ‘Telamonian’, ‘son of Telamon’, tells this Ajax from the other, and μέγας ‘great’ is part of the formula.

sentences.t:
ὢ πόποι ἤδη μέν κε καὶ ὃς μάλα νήπιός ἐστι
γνοίη ὅτι Τρώεσσι πατὴρ Ζεὺς αὐτὸς ἀρήγει.
sentences.l:
“Ah! already even one who is very foolish
would know that father Zeus himself helps the Trojans.
sentences.i: “Ah, even a very foolish man would know by now that father Zeus himself is helping the Trojans.
sentences.n: Ajax speaks. ὢ πόποι ‘Ah’ is an exclamation of dismay. ἤδη μέν κε … γνοίη ‘would already know’: γνοίη is the aorist optative of γιγνώσκω, with κε. ὃς μάλα νήπιός ἐστι is ‘who is very foolish’, and ὅτι ‘that’ opens what he would know. ἀρήγει is ‘helps’, with the dative Τρώεσσι.
sentences.mark: Ajax sees that Zeus favours the Trojans

sentences.t:
τῶν μὲν γὰρ πάντων βέλε’ ἅπτεται ὅς τις ἀφήῃ
ἢ κακὸς ἢ ἀγαθός·
sentences.l:
For of those, of all, the shafts reach their mark, whoever lets fly,
either base or good;
sentences.i: For the shafts of all of them hit home, whoever lets them fly, whether a base man or a good one;
sentences.n: τῶν … πάντων ‘of all of them’ are the Trojans. βέλε’ is βέλεα ‘shafts’, a neuter plural with a singular verb, as often in Greek; ἅπτεται, from ἅπτω, means ‘fastens on’, so ‘reaches its mark’. ὅς τις ἀφήῃ is ‘whoever lets fly’, with ἀφήῃ an aorist subjunctive of ἀφίημι. ἢ κακὸς ἢ ἀγαθός ‘either base or good’: of men in battle the pair means cowardly or brave.

sentences.t: Ζεὺς δ’ ἔμπης πάντ’ ἰθύνει·
sentences.l: but Zeus, all the same, guides all things straight;
sentences.i: but Zeus, all the same, guides everything straight;
sentences.n: ἔμπης is ‘all the same’, and ἰθύνει is the present of ἰθύνω ‘make straight, guide’. πάντ’ is ‘all things’, best taken as all the Trojans’ shafts. The point is the reason for the line before: any man’s shaft finds its mark, because Zeus guides it.

sentences.t: ἡμῖν δ’ αὔτως πᾶσιν ἐτώσια πίπτει ἔραζε.
sentences.l: and for us, just so, for all, in vain they fall to the ground.
sentences.i: while for all of us they simply fall to the ground in vain.
sentences.n: ἡμῖν … πᾶσιν ‘for all of us’ is a dative of the persons concerned. The subject, our shafts, is understood from βέλε’ above. ἐτώσια ‘in vain’ is a neuter plural used as an adverb, and αὔτως ‘just so’ is kept as in earlier parts. ἔραζε is ‘to the ground’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγετ’ αὐτοί περ φραζώμεθα μῆτιν ἀρίστην,
ἠμὲν ὅπως τὸν νεκρὸν ἐρύσσομεν, ἠδὲ καὶ αὐτοὶ
χάρμα φίλοις ἑτάροισι γενώμεθα νοστήσαντες,
sentences.l:
But come, ourselves let us plan the best cunning,
both how the corpse we may drag, and also ourselves
a joy to dear companions may become, having returned home,
sentences.i: But come, let us ourselves plan the best stroke of cunning: both how we may drag the corpse away, and how we ourselves may come home and be a joy to our dear companions,
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγετ’ ‘but come’ introduces φραζώμεθα, a hortatory subjunctive of φράζομαι ‘plan’. μῆτις is skilful scheming, ‘cunning’, and with φράζομαι ‘plan’ it reads ‘plan the best cunning’; the English layer gives ‘a stroke of cunning’ so that it reads as prose. ἠμὲν … ἠδέ is ‘both … and’; ἐρύσσομεν is a short-vowel subjunctive, ‘we may drag’, and τὸν νεκρόν is Patroclus’ body. γενώμεθα is another subjunctive, and νοστήσαντες is the aorist participle of νοστέω ‘return home’.

sentences.t:
οἵ που δεῦρ’ ὁρόωντες ἀκηχέδατ’, οὐδ’ ἔτι φασὶν
Ἕκτορος ἀνδροφόνοιο μένος καὶ χεῖρας ἀάπτους
σχήσεσθ’, ἀλλ’ ἐν νηυσὶ μελαίνῃσιν πεσέεσθαι.
sentences.l:
who somewhere, here looking on, are grieved, and no longer, they say,
will we hold back the might of man-slaying Hector, and his untouchable hands,
but in the black ships will fall.
sentences.i: who, I suppose, are grieved as they look this way; and they say that we shall no longer hold back the might of man-slaying Hector and his irresistible hands, but shall fall at the black ships.
sentences.n: οἵ are the companions at home; που is ‘I suppose’, and ἀκηχέδατ’ is an old perfect form, ‘they are grieved’. φασίν ‘they say’ takes the infinitives σχήσεσθ’ and πεσέεσθαι (future infinitives), with ‘we’ understood; σχήσεσθαι is ‘hold back’, with the object μένος … καὶ χεῖρας. ἀάπτους: the meaning is not known, and ‘untouchable’ and ‘irresistible’ are traditional guesses. The last line stands earlier in the poem with the Trojans as subject, and the English there says ‘upon the black ships’; here the Achaeans are the ones who fall at the ships, so the wording is changed.

sentences.t:
εἴη δ’ ὅς τις ἑταῖρος ἀπαγγείλειε τάχιστα
Πηλεΐδῃ, ἐπεὶ οὔ μιν ὀΐομαι οὐδὲ πεπύσθαι
λυγρῆς ἀγγελίης, ὅτι οἱ φίλος ὤλεθ’ ἑταῖρος.
sentences.l:
May there be some companion who would report most quickly
to Peleus’-son, since I do not think he has even learned
of the grievous news, that his dear companion has perished.
sentences.i: If only some companion could take word as quickly as possible to the son of Peleus; for I do not think he has even heard the grievous news, that his dear companion has perished.
sentences.n: εἴη is an optative of wish, ‘may there be’, and ὅς τις ἑταῖρος ἀπαγγείλειε is a relative clause with the optative, ‘a companion who would report’. Πηλεΐδῃ ‘to the son of Peleus’ is Achilles, named by his patronymic. πεπύσθαι is the perfect infinitive of πυνθάνομαι ‘learn’, with λυγρῆς ἀγγελίης ‘the grievous news’ in the genitive. ὅτι opens what the news is, and ὤλεθ’ is ὤλετο ‘perished’; the dear companion is Patroclus.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ οὔ πῃ δύναμαι ἰδέειν τοιοῦτον Ἀχαιῶν·
sentences.l: But in no way can I see such a one of the Achaeans;
sentences.i: But nowhere can I see such a man among the Achaeans;
sentences.n: οὔ πῃ ‘in no way, nowhere’ and ἰδέειν, the epic aorist infinitive of ὁράω ‘see’. τοιοῦτον ‘such a one’ is the messenger Ajax wants, and the next line gives the reason he cannot be seen.

sentences.t: ἠέρι γὰρ κατέχονται ὁμῶς αὐτοί τε καὶ ἵπποι.
sentences.l: for in mist are held, alike, both the men themselves and the horses.
sentences.i: for men and horses alike are wrapped in mist.
sentences.n: ἠέρι is the dative of ἠήρ ‘mist’, with κατέχονται ‘are held down, are covered’. αὐτοί here means ‘the men themselves’, set against ἵπποι ‘horses’, and ὁμῶς is ‘alike’.

sentences.t:
Ζεῦ πάτερ ἀλλὰ σὺ ῥῦσαι ὑπ’ ἠέρος υἷας Ἀχαιῶν,
ποίησον δ’ αἴθρην, δὸς δ’ ὀφθαλμοῖσιν ἰδέσθαι·
sentences.l:
Father Zeus, but do you rescue from the mist the sons of the Achaeans,
and make clear sky, and grant to the eyes to see;
sentences.i: Father Zeus, do you rescue the sons of the Achaeans from the mist, make a clear sky, and let our eyes see;
sentences.n: Ajax now prays. Ζεῦ πάτερ is ‘Father Zeus’, the vocative. ῥῦσαι is the aorist imperative middle of ῥύομαι ‘rescue’, and ὑπ’ ἠέρος is ‘from under the mist’; υἷας is the epic accusative plural of υἱός. αἴθρην is ‘clear sky, bright air’, and δὸς ὀφθαλμοῖσιν ἰδέσθαι is ‘grant to the eyes to see’, ἰδέσθαι being the aorist infinitive middle of ὁράω.

sentences.t: ἐν δὲ φάει καὶ ὄλεσσον, ἐπεί νύ τοι εὔαδεν οὕτως.
sentences.l: and in the light even destroy us, since now it has so pleased you.”
sentences.i: and destroy us even in the light, since it has so pleased you.”
sentences.n: φάος ‘light’ is daylight here. ὄλεσσον is the aorist imperative of ὄλλυμι ‘destroy’, with ‘us’ understood, and καὶ is ‘even’. εὔαδεν is the aorist of ἁνδάνω ‘please’ (the augmented, old form), so ἐπεί νύ τοι εὔαδεν οὕτως is ‘since it has so pleased you’. The prayer asks only to die in daylight, not blind in the mist.

sentences.t: ὣς φάτο, τὸν δὲ πατὴρ ὀλοφύρατο δάκρυ χέοντα·
sentences.l: So he spoke, and him the father grieved for, a tear shedding;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the Father grieved for him as he shed tears;
sentences.n: ὣς φάτο closes Ajax’s speech. πατήρ ‘the Father’ is Zeus, just addressed; ὀλοφύρατο is the aorist of ὀλοφύρομαι ‘grieve for’, and δάκρυ χέοντα ‘shedding a tear’ is accusative, agreeing with τόν (Ajax). The line stands also at 8.245, where Zeus pities Agamemnon in tears.

sentences.t:
αὐτίκα δ’ ἠέρα μὲν σκέδασεν καὶ ἀπῶσεν ὀμίχλην,
ἠέλιος δ’ ἐπέλαμψε, μάχη δ’ ἐπὶ πᾶσα φαάνθη·
sentences.l:
At once the mist he scattered and drove away the fog,
and the sun shone upon them, and the whole battle came into view;
sentences.i: At once he scattered the mist and drove away the fog; the sun shone out, and the whole battle came into view;
sentences.n: σκέδασεν is the aorist of σκεδάννυμι ‘scatter’, and ἀπῶσεν the aorist of ἀπωθέω ‘push away’. ἠέρα and ὀμίχλην are two words for mist, here ‘mist’ and ‘fog’. ἠέλιος is the sun (Attic ἥλιος). ἐπέλαμψε is the aorist of ἐπιλάμπω ‘shine upon’, and φαάνθη the aorist passive of φαίνω, ‘was made visible’, with ἐπί split from its verb (tmesis) and πᾶσα ‘whole’ agreeing with μάχη.

sentences.t: καὶ τότ’ ἄρ’ Αἴας εἶπε βοὴν ἀγαθὸν Μενέλαον·
sentences.l: And then Ajax said to Menelaus, good at the war-cry:
sentences.i: Then Ajax said to Menelaus, good at the war-cry:
sentences.n: βοὴν ἀγαθόν ‘good at the war-cry’ is a stock epithet of Menelaus, translated the same way every time; the accusative βοήν says in what he is good.

sentences.t:
σκέπτεο νῦν Μενέλαε διοτρεφὲς αἴ κεν ἴδηαι
ζωὸν ἔτ’ Ἀντίλοχον μεγαθύμου Νέστορος υἱόν,
ὄτρυνον δ’ Ἀχιλῆϊ δαΐφρονι θᾶσσον ἰόντα
εἰπεῖν ὅττι ῥά οἱ πολὺ φίλτατος ὤλεθ’ ἑταῖρος.
sentences.l:
“Look about now, Menelaus, Zeus-nurtured one, if you may see
still alive Antilochus, the son of great-hearted Nestor,
and urge him to go more quickly to Achilles, wise-minded,
to say that by far the dearest to him a companion has perished.”
sentences.i: “Look about now, Menelaus, Zeus-nurtured one, in case you can see Antilochus, the son of great-hearted Nestor, still alive, and urge him to go as quickly as he can to wise-hearted Achilles and tell him that his dearest companion by far has perished.”
sentences.n: σκέπτεο is the imperative of σκέπτομαι ‘look about’, and αἴ κεν ἴδηαι is ‘in case you may see’ (aorist subjunctive). διοτρεφές ‘Zeus-nurtured’ is a stock epithet of kings, here a vocative. ὄτρυνον is the imperative of ὀτρύνω ‘urge on’; ἰόντα, accusative, agrees with Antilochus, and θᾶσσον is ‘more quickly’. δαΐφρονι, ‘wise-minded’, is the stock epithet of Achilles here, and whether it means ‘wise’ or ‘fierce’ is disputed. In εἰπεῖν ὅττι ‘to say that’, ὅττι is ὅτι; πολὺ φίλτατος is ‘by far the dearest’.
sentences.mark: Ajax sends Menelaus to look for Antilochus

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’, οὐδ’ ἀπίθησε βοὴν ἀγαθὸς Μενέλαος,
sentences.l: So he spoke, and did not disobey, Menelaus, good at the war-cry,
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Menelaus, good at the war-cry, did not disobey;
sentences.n: A new paragraph. ὣς ἔφατ’, οὐδ’ ἀπίθησε ‘so he spoke, and he did not disobey’ is a formula of obedience; ἀπίθησε is the aorist of ἀπιθέω ‘disobey’. The unit ends at a comma because the sentence goes on into the simile.

sentences.t:
βῆ δ’ ἰέναι ὥς τίς τε λέων ἀπὸ μεσσαύλοιο,
ὅς τ’ ἐπεὶ ἄρ κε κάμῃσι κύνας τ’ ἄνδρας τ’ ἐρεθίζων,
sentences.l:
He set out to go, like some lion from the farmyard,
who, when he has grown weary of provoking dogs and men,
sentences.i: He set out like a lion going away from the farmyard, one that has grown weary of provoking dogs and men,
sentences.n: βῆ δ’ ἰέναι ‘set out to go’ opens a journey, and ὥς τίς τε λέων begins a simile that runs to line 664. μεσσαύλοιο is the genitive of μέσσαυλος, a farmyard. ὅς τ’ ἐπεὶ ἄρ κε κάμῃσι is a general relative clause with the aorist subjunctive, ‘who, whenever he has grown weary’, and ἐρεθίζων ‘provoking’ is a participle governing κύνας and ἄνδρας. Menelaus is the lion, and the dogs and men are the Trojans.

sentences.t:
οἵ τέ μιν οὐκ εἰῶσι βοῶν ἐκ πῖαρ ἑλέσθαι
πάννυχοι ἐγρήσσοντες·
sentences.l:
who do not let him take the fat from the cattle,
all night keeping awake;
sentences.i: and these, keeping awake all night, will not let him take the fat of the cattle;
sentences.n: οἵ are the dogs and men of the line before, and μιν is the lion. εἰῶσι is the present of ἐάω ‘allow’ in its epic form, and πῖαρ is ‘fat’. ἐγρήσσοντες ‘keeping awake’ is a participle of ἐγρήσσω, and πάννυχοι ‘all night’ goes with it. These two lines stand also in the lion simile of Book 11, there said of Ajax.

sentences.t:
ὃ δὲ κρειῶν ἐρατίζων
ἰθύει, ἀλλ’ οὔ τι πρήσσει·
sentences.l:
but he, for flesh longing,
charges straight on, but accomplishes nothing;
sentences.i: But he, longing for flesh, charges straight on, but accomplishes nothing;
sentences.n: ὃ is the lion. κρειῶν is the genitive plural of κρέας ‘flesh’, the object of ἐρατίζων ‘longing for’. ἰθύει is ‘charges straight on’, and πρήσσει ‘accomplishes’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of the line.

sentences.t:
θαμέες γὰρ ἄκοντες
ἀντίον ἀΐσσουσι θρασειάων ἀπὸ χειρῶν,
καιόμεναί τε δεταί, τάς τε τρεῖ ἐσσύμενός περ·
sentences.i: for close-set javelins fly against him from bold hands, and so do burning torches, from which he flinches, though he is hurrying on;
sentences.n: θαμέες ‘close-set’ and ἄκοντες ‘javelins’ are the subject; ἀΐσσουσι is ‘dart’, and θρασειάων is the feminine genitive plural of θρασύς ‘bold’, with χειρῶν ‘hands’. καιόμεναί is ‘burning’ and δεταί are ‘torches’. τάς τε τρεῖ is ‘from which he trembles’ (τρέω), and ἐσσύμενος περ is ‘hurrying though he is’.

sentences.t: ἠῶθεν δ’ ἀπονόσφιν ἔβη τετιηότι θυμῷ·
sentences.l: and at dawn away, apart, he went with grieved heart;
sentences.i: and at dawn he goes off, away, grieved at heart;
sentences.n: ἠῶθεν is ‘at dawn’ and ἀπονόσφιν ‘away, apart’, printed here as one word. ἔβη is an aorist used for what the lion always does (a general statement). τετιηότι is the perfect participle of a verb meaning ‘be grieved’, and agrees with θυμῷ.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἀπὸ Πατρόκλοιο βοὴν ἀγαθὸς Μενέλαος
ἤϊε πόλλ’ ἀέκων·
sentences.l:
So from Patroclus Menelaus, good at the war-cry,
went, much unwilling;
sentences.i: So Menelaus, good at the war-cry, went away from Patroclus, very unwilling;
sentences.n: ὣς answers the ὥς of the simile: Menelaus goes like the lion. ἤϊε is the imperfect of εἶμι ‘go’, and πόλλ’ ἀέκων is ‘very unwilling’, with πολλά used as an adverb and ἀέκων ‘unwilling’.

sentences.t:
περὶ γὰρ δίε μή μιν Ἀχαιοὶ
ἀργαλέου πρὸ φόβοιο ἕλωρ δηΐοισι λίποιεν.
sentences.l:
for greatly he feared lest him the Achaeans
before grievous flight a prey to enemies should leave.
sentences.i: for he feared greatly that, in the face of grievous flight, the Achaeans might leave him as prey for the enemy.
sentences.n: περὶ γὰρ δίε ‘for greatly he feared’: δίε is a past tense of δείδω (poetic δίω) ‘fear’, and μή … λίποιεν ‘lest they leave’ is an aorist optative after a past verb. μιν is Patroclus’ body. ἀργαλέου πρὸ φόβοιο is ‘in the face of grievous flight’, with ἀργαλέος ‘grievous’; ἕλωρ is ‘prey’ and δηΐοισι ‘to the enemy’.

sentences.t: πολλὰ δὲ Μηριόνῃ τε καὶ Αἰάντεσσ’ ἐπέτελλεν·
sentences.l: And much to Meriones and to the Ajaxes he laid charge:
sentences.i: He laid many charges on Meriones and the Ajaxes:
sentences.n: ἐπέτελλεν is the imperfect of ἐπιτέλλω ‘lay a charge on’, with πολλά ‘many things’. Αἰάντεσσ’ is the dative plural of Αἴας, ‘the Ajaxes’, the two heroes of that name, as the dual in the next line shows.

sentences.t:
Αἴαντ’ Ἀργείων ἡγήτορε Μηριόνη τε
νῦν τις ἐνηείης Πατροκλῆος δειλοῖο
μνησάσθω·
sentences.i: “Ajaxes, you two leaders of the Argives, and Meriones, now let each of you remember the kindness of miserable Patroclus;
sentences.n: Αἴαντ’ ἡγήτορε are duals, ‘you two Ajaxes, leaders’, and Μηριόνη τε adds the third; Ἀργείων is ‘of the Argives’. τις is ‘someone, each one’. ἐνηείης is the genitive of ἐνηείη ‘kindness’, a rare noun, and μνησάσθω the aorist imperative middle of μιμνῄσκομαι ‘remember’, which takes the genitive. δειλοῖο ‘miserable’ is here a word of pity for the dead man.

sentences.t:
πᾶσιν γὰρ ἐπίστατο μείλιχος εἶναι
ζωὸς ἐών· νῦν αὖ θάνατος καὶ μοῖρα κιχάνει.
sentences.l:
for to all he knew how to be gentle
while living; but now death and fate overtake him.”
sentences.i: for he knew how to be gentle to everyone while he lived; but now death and fate overtake him.”
sentences.n: ἐπίστατο ‘he knew how’ takes the infinitive εἶναι, and μείλιχος is ‘gentle’. ζωὸς ἐών is ‘while living’ (ἐών is ὤν). νῦν αὖ is ‘but now, in turn’. Two subjects, θάνατος καὶ μοῖρα, share the one singular verb κιχάνει ‘overtakes’.
